summary: Describes a general syntax for data that may have cryptography applied to it, such as digital signatures and digital envelopes. It is an informational copy of an RSA Laboratories standard that later formed the basis for the Cryptographic Message Syntax.

plainLanguage.summary: A kind of envelope for secret messages. It can hold a signature to show who sent it and a lock so only the right person can open it.

questions: what is the difference between signed data and enveloped data
subtitle: A general envelope format for data that can be signed, encrypted, digested or any nesting of those.

tldr.problem: Applications that sign or encrypt data need one agreed way to package the data together with signatures, encrypted keys, certificates and algorithm names.
tldr.mechanism: PKCS #7 defines a ContentInfo wrapper in ASN.1 that names a content type and carries the content. Six content types (data, signed, enveloped, signed-and-enveloped, digested, encrypted) can be nested inside one another.
tldr.outcome: RFC 2315 is an Informational copy of an RSA Laboratories specification, version 1.5. It leaves key management policy and text re-encoding of the binary output to other documents.

today: RFC 2315 is an Informational RFC published in March 1998, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records version 1.5 of a specification from RSA Laboratories rather than an IETF standard.

sections.title: What PKCS #7 Describes
sections.content:
RFC 2315 describes a general syntax for data that may have cryptography applied to it, such as digital signatures and digital envelopes. It is version 1.5 of PKCS #7, published by RSA Laboratories.

The syntax admits recursion: one envelope can be nested inside another, or one party can sign data that was previously enveloped. It also lets arbitrary attributes, such as signing time, be authenticated along with the message content, and lets other attributes such as countersignatures be attached to a signature. A degenerate case of the syntax is a way to distribute certificates and certificate-revocation lists.

The scope is deliberately narrow. The document is compatible with Privacy-Enhanced Mail (PEM), but decisions such as which certificate issuers are top-level or what policies issuers follow are left outside it. The output is meant to be BER-encoded binary, and the document does not say how to re-encode it as text for mail systems that cannot carry arbitrary octets.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a standard way to pack a message with signatures and locks so anyone who follows the rules can unpack it. It does not decide who you should trust.

sections.title: ContentInfo and the Six Content Types
sections.content:
Everything is wrapped in one exported type, ContentInfo. It has a contentType, which is an object identifier, and an optional content whose type depends on the identifier. If the content is omitted, its value must be supplied by other means. This makes "external signatures" possible, where the signed content is not copied into the structure.

The RFC defines six content types in two classes. The base class holds just data, with no cryptographic enhancements. The enhanced class holds content of some type, possibly encrypted, plus enhancements. Enhanced types encapsulate other content, which gives the terms "outer" content (the one with the enhancements) and "inner" content (the one being enhanced).

The enhanced types are designed so they can be prepared in a single pass using indefinite-length BER encoding and processed in a single pass in any BER encoding. Because DER is required by signed-data, signed-and-enveloped-data and digested-data, an extra pass may be needed when the inner content is not plain data.
sections.plainLanguage: Every package has a label saying what kind of box it is, then the contents. Some boxes hold plain stuff, and others hold another box plus a signature or a lock.

sections.title: Signed Data
sections.content:
The signed-data type holds content of any type plus encrypted message digests of that content for zero or more signers. A signer's encrypted digest is the digital signature. Any content can be signed by any number of signers in parallel.

To build it, a message digest is computed for each signer with that signer's digest algorithm, then encrypted with the signer's private key and collected into a SignerInfo, along with certificates and certificate-revocation lists. A recipient decrypts each encrypted digest with the signer's public key and compares the result to an independently computed digest. The public key is either in a certificate in the message or named by the issuer's distinguished name and a serial number.

A SignerInfo may include authenticatedAttributes, which are signed along with the content. If present, they must include a PKCS #9 content-type attribute and a PKCS #9 message-digest attribute. Unauthenticated attributes, such as countersignatures, are not covered by the signature. With no signers at all, the structure is just a carrier for certificates and certificate-revocation lists.

The digest is wrapped in a DigestInfo that also names the digest algorithm. The RFC explains this limits the damage if one digest algorithm is compromised, using MD2 versus MD5 as its example.
sections.plainLanguage: Signing is like putting a fingerprint of your message on it, sealed with something only you have. Anyone can check that the fingerprint still matches the message.

sections.title: Enveloped, Digested and Encrypted Data
sections.content:
The enveloped-data type builds a digital envelope. A content-encryption key is generated at random, encrypted separately with each recipient's public key, and the content is encrypted with that content-encryption key. Each recipient gets a RecipientInfo with the encrypted key. At least one recipient is required.

For algorithms that need input in multiples of k octets, the RFC specifies padding at the trailing end with k - (l mod k) octets, each of that value, where l is the input length. This is well defined only if k is below 256.

The signed-and-enveloped-data type combines both, and its signed digest is encrypted a second time with the content-encryption key so an adversary cannot test guesses of the content against the digest. The RFC notes that signed-data followed by enveloped-data is generally preferable, except for compatibility with the PEM ENCRYPTED process type.

The digested-data type adds a message digest to content to add integrity. The encrypted-data type has no recipients and no encrypted keys; keys are managed by other means, and the typical use is encrypting data for local storage, perhaps with a password as the key.
sections.plainLanguage: An envelope uses one secret key for the message, then locks that key separately for each person who should read it. A digest is just a fingerprint, and encrypted data is a locked box with no key sent along.

sections.title: Versions, Object Identifiers and PEM Compatibility
sections.content:
Versions 1.0 to 1.3 were distributed at PKCS meetings in February and March 1991. Version 1.4 was part of the June 3, 1991 initial public release. Version 1.5 adds the CertificateRevocationLists type, lets signed data carry CRLs or carry certificates alone, adds the PEM-compatible digest encryption process, describes the padding method and adds the encrypted-data type.

The seven object identifiers hang from pkcs-7, which is { iso(1) member-body(2) US(840) rsadsi(113549) pkcs(1) 7 }. Data, signedData, envelopedData, signedAndEnvelopedData, digestedData and encryptedData are numbered 1 to 6 beneath it.

Signed-data can be converted to and from PEM messages without cryptographic operations when the content is data, there are no authenticated attributes, the digest is md2 or md5 and RSA encryption from PKCS #1 is used. The security section says only that security issues are discussed throughout the memo.
sections.plainLanguage: The format grew over several versions, and each content type has its own number so a reader knows which kind of box it is holding.

viz.caption: THE SIX CONTENT TYPES AND THEIR OBJECT IDENTIFIERS

items.label: data
items.desc: An arbitrary octet string; the only base-class type.

items.label: signedData
items.desc: Content plus encrypted digests for zero or more signers.

items.label: envelopedData
items.desc: Encrypted content plus the content key encrypted for each recipient.

items.label: signedAndEnvelopedData
items.desc: Signatures and envelopes combined, with doubly encrypted digests.

items.label: digestedData
items.desc: Content plus a message digest of it.

items.label: encryptedData
items.desc: Encrypted content with keys managed by other means.
